summaries.example: Imagine two cards: one says “There is a 40% chance I will get the job,” and the other says “There is a 60% chance I will not get the job.” They describe the same chances, but the first may feel more hopeful. The different wording can affect what people believe or choose. Hyperintensionality studies cases like this, where the way an idea is presented matters even when two statements are true in exactly the same possible situations.
summaries.summary: Hyperintensionality is the study of differences between ideas that ordinary possible-world comparisons can miss. Two statements are necessarily equivalent when they are true in all the same ways things could be. For example, “Mike is Mike” and “Mike is Jack the Ripper,” if the names refer to the same person, may be true in the same possible worlds. Yet learning the second statement could be important information, while the first is not. Similar differences appear in belief, knowledge, imagination, meaning, conditionals, mathematics, explanations, essence, and grounding. The entry also describes several proposed tools, including topics or subject matter, structured meanings, impossible worlds, relevant logic, and truthmaker approaches. Philosophers disagree about whether these differences are genuine features of meaning and reality or results of human thinking and conversation.
key_ideas: Two statements can be true in exactly the same possible situations but still seem to say different things.
Belief, knowledge, information, meaning, and explanation may care about how an idea is expressed.
Some philosophers try to explain these differences using possible worlds; others think we need finer tools.
There is no single agreed theory of how fine-grained these differences should be.
summaries.why_it_matters: The way an idea is expressed can affect learning, decisions, explanations, and communication. Studying hyperintensionality helps philosophers ask why a logical truth can still be surprising, why equivalent sentences may not feel equally informative, and why some explanations work while others do not. It also shows that “having the same truth value” may not be enough to describe everything people think and say.

important_terms.definition: A way of telling apart meanings or ideas that would be true in all the same possible situations.
A way things could be, or could have been. Philosophers use these to compare statements.
What a sentence says or means in a particular setting.
Knowing something without needing to learn it from experience, such as knowing a simple rule of arithmetic.
A connection in which one fact helps explain why another fact is true.

questions_to_think_about: Can two sentences be equally true but give different information?
Does changing the wording of an idea change what you believe?
When does one fact really explain another?
Should a person be expected to know every logical result of what they already know?

summaries.example: Suppose a student knows that water is identical to H2O but has not yet investigated chemistry. The student may be certain that water is water while remaining unsure that water is H2O. If belief were sensitive only to truth at possible worlds, these necessarily equivalent claims would be interchangeable. The example suggests that belief can depend on the concepts, words, or representational routes through which a claim is grasped. This is one reason hyperintensional theories distinguish more finely than standard possible-worlds semantics.
summaries.summary: Hyperintensionality concerns concepts and operators that distinguish contents more finely than necessary equivalence. In standard possible-worlds semantics, a proposition is often represented by the set of possible worlds where it is true. This is powerful, but it can collapse distinctions that seem important. A tautology and a difficult mathematical result may be true at every possible world while differing in informativeness. “Mike is Mike” and “Mike is Jack the Ripper” may likewise be necessarily equivalent while differing in what someone can learn. Belief and knowledge create a related problem: if knowledge were simply truth throughout the agent’s accessible worlds, it would seem to include every logical consequence and every logical truth, producing logical omniscience. The entry surveys representational and worldly phenomena, including meaning, conditionals, fiction, essence, grounding, explanation, dispositions, chance, ethics, and truthmakers. It also presents disagreements about whether hyperintensional intuitions are reliable. Some philosophers defend finer-grained semantics; others appeal to language, cognitive fragmentation, or misleading heuristics. The remaining challenge is to determine how much structure a theory needs and whether one framework can explain all the cases.
key_ideas: Extensional operators preserve truth under substitution of expressions with the same truth value; intensional operators preserve it under substitution of necessarily equivalent contents. Hyperintensional operators can fail even at that stronger level.

The problem appears in intentional concepts such as belief, knowledge, imagination, and information. Standard possible-worlds accounts can imply logical omniscience: knowing one claim would require knowing all its logical consequences.

It also appears in semantic concepts. Propositions represented only by truth sets may identify a trivial necessary truth with a significant mathematical theorem, or identify distinct topics that happen to be true everywhere.

Worldly cases include essence, grounding, explanation, intrinsicness, dispositions, chance, obligations, and truthmakers. Whether these are genuinely worldly or instead depend on representation remains disputed.

Proposed approaches include two-dimensional semantics, subject-matter theories, structured propositions, impossible worlds, relevant logic, exact truthmaker semantics, and algebraic or object-theoretic systems.
A central difficulty is granularity: a theory must distinguish enough to model belief and explanation without making every syntactic variation a different meaning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hyperintensionality matters because truth conditions alone may not capture information, understanding, reasoning, or explanation. It can clarify why equivalent formulations can guide belief differently, why a proof can teach something even when its conclusion is necessarily true, and why “because” is not interchangeable in both directions. The debate also connects formal logic with language, artificial intelligence, decision-making, epistemology, and metaphysics.

important_terms.definition: A property of an operator or concept that can distinguish necessarily equivalent contents; substitution of such contents may change truth value.
A standard semantic framework that represents a proposition by the possible worlds in which it is true.
Two contents are necessarily equivalent when they are true at exactly the same possible worlds.
A sentence-position, such as “believes that” or “is essential,” where replacing one expression with another can affect truth.
A proposition’s subject or issue—what it is about—which can add information beyond its possible-world truth conditions.
The view that propositions have parts or structure, rather than being only sets of worlds.
A way of modeling distinctions by adding ways things could not be, as well as possible worlds.
The idea that rough cognitive methods can create misleading intuitions, so a theory may add distinctions merely to fit bad evidence.

questions_to_think_about: If two claims are true in every possible world, can one still be more informative than the other?
Does a person who knows a theorem automatically know every logical consequence of it?
Are differences in explanation features of the world, features of language, or both?
Would adding impossible worlds solve the problems, or simply move them elsewhere?
How fine-grained should meanings be: sentence-by-sentence, or coarser than syntax?

summaries.example: A school newsletter offers two descriptions of the same quiz result: “You have a 75% chance of passing” and “You have a 25% chance of failing.” The numbers match, but students may react differently to the two descriptions. One sounds encouraging; the other sounds worrying. The claims are necessarily equivalent in the relevant sense, yet the framing can affect belief and choice. This is a familiar kind of hyperintensional difference.
summaries.summary: Hyperintensionality asks whether some meanings and philosophical concepts distinguish between statements that standard modal semantics treats as equivalent. Two statements are necessarily equivalent when they are true at the same possible worlds. Yet equivalent statements can differ in information, subject matter, belief, explanation, or practical effect. A person may know a simple mathematical principle without knowing a difficult consequence of it. A statement that is true in every possible world can still be a major discovery, while another necessary truth may be trivial. The entry separates representational phenomena—belief, knowledge, imagination, information, meaning, and conditionals—from worldly phenomena such as essence, grounding, explanation, intrinsic properties, dispositions, chance, and truthmakers. Some philosophers argue that possible-worlds methods can be supplemented or that our intuitions are distorted by context and cognitive shortcuts. Others argue that the distinctions are systematic and need richer semantics. Suggested frameworks include topics, structured propositions, impossible worlds, relevant logic, two-dimensional semantics, and exact truthmaker approaches. A major unresolved issue is granularity: a theory should distinguish genuinely different contents without treating every difference in wording as a different meaning.
key_ideas: Standard possible-worlds semantics groups statements together when they are true at the same possible worlds, but many philosophical cases seem to require more distinctions.
Belief and knowledge may not include every logical consequence of what someone knows. This is called the problem of logical omniscience.
Information is not just a matter of ruling out possible worlds: learning a difficult theorem can be informative even if the theorem is necessarily true.
Meaning may involve subject matter or internal structure. “2 + 2 = 4” and “Every equilateral triangle is equiangular” can both be necessary without saying the same thing.
Philosophers disagree about whether hyperintensional differences belong to language and thought, to the world itself, or to misleading habits of reasoning.
Theories try different solutions, including two-dimensional meanings, structured propositions, impossible worlds, relevant logic, and truthmaker semantics.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic links abstract logic to ordinary reasoning. It helps explain framing effects, limits on what people know, the difference between a proof and a bare theorem, and why an explanation can be correct in one direction but not the reverse. It also matters for designing theories of language, knowledge, artificial intelligence, and metaphysical dependence.

important_terms.definition: A distinction between contents that remain even when the contents are true in all the same possible situations.
A complete way things might have been, used to compare when statements are true or false.
The truth value or set of possible worlds associated with a statement in standard semantics.
A mental state directed toward something, such as believing, knowing, imagining, or hoping that a claim is true.
The meaning or expressed idea of a sentence, not merely whether the sentence is true.
The subject or issue a sentence concerns, such as a person, event, or mathematical problem.
The claim that one fact or state of affairs accounts for, or makes intelligible, another.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a person accept one formulation of a claim but not recognize an equivalent formulation?
Should knowing a fact require knowing all of its logical consequences?
Can two statements have the same truth conditions but different topics?
Is a good explanation determined by the facts, by human interests, or by both?
What would count as too much detail in a theory of meaning?
